memory_update.text: For broad Technology/AI infrastructure work, first separate visible demand anchors from hidden supply-chain constraints; mega-cap chip and cloud leaders should be context, not the center of the underfollowed discovery funnel.

High-end AI-server MLCCs and their upstream dielectric powders are promising underfollowed nodes because the relevant bottleneck appears to be narrow product-grade capability rather than commodity MLCC volume.
Advanced package substrates and ABF build-up film should be tracked as a distinct AI accelerator chokepoint separate from foundry capacity and GPU design leadership.
Inspection, metrology, and process-control tools benefit from rising AI chip and packaging complexity across multiple customers, making this a cross-winner infrastructure node.
Data-center electrical and thermal component suppliers are a second-order AI infrastructure lane where smaller industrial companies may be hidden under non-technology sector labels.

Cybersecurity and cloud software were not sufficiently evidenced in this pass and require a separate decomposition focused on identity, cloud security, API security, OT security, AI security, observability, and compliance automation.
Current market pricing, analyst coverage, customer concentration, and company-specific financial exposure must be checked before promoting any node candidates to a ranked Layer 2 universe.

layer1a.summary: Layer 1A decomposition of the broad Technology theme suggests the best next research path is not to start with mega-cap AI/cloud leaders, but to map the second-order supply chain around AI infrastructure buildout: high-end passive components, MLCC dielectric powders, advanced package substrates/build-up film, process-control equipment, data-center electrical/thermal infrastructure, and supply-chain coordination software. The highest-quality underfollowed lanes appear where AI demand creates qualification-heavy, capacity-constrained, or supplier-concentrated chokepoints that are one or two steps removed from obvious GPU/cloud beneficiaries.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The bottleneck is not generic MLCC capacity, but the narrow class of small, high-capacitance, low-ESR, low-ESL parts suitable for dense AI accelerator boards.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer companies with meaningful high-end MLCC exposure, server/datacenter disclosures, or electronic-materials margin mix shift. Small/mid-cap opportunities may exist among regional component makers but require customer and product-grade verification.

demand_drivers: AI accelerator deployment by hyperscalers and cloud providers requiring denser server boards, more power delivery, higher-speed networking, and more advanced packaging.

Advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration growth as AI performance increasingly depends on chiplet, HBM, substrate, interconnect, and yield complexity rather than only front-end transistor scaling.
Data-center power density growth driving demand for electrical infrastructure, thermal management, power components, grid interconnection, and reliability engineering.
Semiconductor manufacturing complexity increasing inspection, metrology, process-control, yield-management, and advanced packaging process-control demand.
Supply-chain volatility and component scarcity creating demand for better supplier visibility, planning, and automation software in electronics and industrial manufacturing.

Cybersecurity and infrastructure software demand likely rising as AI workloads, cloud estates, and industrial automation expand attack surfaces, though this lane requires separate evidence gathering in later layers.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Use a two-lane funnel. First, keep reference leaders such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, KLA, and hyperscalers as demand/context anchors. Second, hunt for small- and mid-cap or lower-attention suppliers with narrower exposure to AI infrastructure bottlenecks: Japanese and Taiwanese electronic-materials suppliers, MLCC feedstock producers, substrate makers, component makers, inspection/metrology sub-suppliers, data-center electrical component vendors, thermal subsystem suppliers, and niche software vendors for supplier coordination. Avoid ranking securities at this layer; instead define nodes and evidence targets for later verification.
supply_side_constraints: Qualification and reliability constraints for components used in AI servers, automotive electronics, data centers, and advanced semiconductor manufacturing.
Concentrated supplier bases in advanced substrates, build-up film, high-end MLCCs, dielectric powders, and process-control tools.
Capacity expansion lead times for advanced packaging substrates, specialty chemicals, MLCC materials, inspection/metrology tools, and data-center electrical equipment.
Customer certification cycles and design-in inertia that can make approved suppliers difficult to replace once qualified.
Manufacturing know-how bottlenecks in sub-100nm barium titanate powders, high-capacitance low-ESR/low-ESL MLCCs, and high-end package substrate materials.
Project execution and grid interconnection bottlenecks limiting how fast compute capacity can be built even when chips are available.
